pages.title: Introduction to COOs
facts: For the production process I advise people read the following article: 12back.com: The Creation Process
In addition, theswca.com also has good information, check out the following article: theswca.com: Steel mould
Then comes the „hard copy“ which is a copy of the original sculpt in a very hard material which is necessary for making the steel moulds.
The so called „steel moulds“ can be made from aluminium, steel or even brass.
The „hardcopy“ is transferred into the mould with kind of a three-dimensional pantograph.
The following is now important for understanding when a coo is placed.
The first figures produced in that mould is the so called „first shot“.
The awarding authority (Kenner) has a look at this „first shot“ and gives its okay for the production.
At this point the moulds first gets duplicated and then stamped and marked!
I have no proof of the following but to me it makes totally sense: The steel-moulds were the original ones, the ones the first shots were made from.
Stamped “Made in Hong Kong“, “Hong Kong“ or “H.K.“. These are normally the unaltered ‘steel moulds', so I call them “original COO's”
Stamped “Made in Taiwan“ or “Taiwan“. These are unaltered coos and also belong to the “original COO's”
Stamped “Macau“, “Macao“ or the country is deleted (no COO). These are altered Hong Kong COO's.
Produced No COO on Han Endor and altered COO on AT-AT Commander
likely bought unassembled and unpainted figures to paint and pack them (early ESB)
likely produced their own figures (mould process plus paint process in later ESB and ROTJ area)
and finally bought finished figures from Mexico (ROTJ) and Taiwan (ESB, ROTJ) to pack them.
Two points I like to add to show how complicated this detective work is

pages.title: Poch Guide
facts: This guide is dedicated to the earliest produced figures in Spain, called “Poch” variants.
The Spanish company Poch (or Novedades Poch) never produced SW action figures on its own.
In July 1980, three companies including Poch merged to form the PBP company, these companies were: Poch, Borras and Palouzie.
PBP used a totally different material compared to their former production and to the rest of the world. Those figures are unique worldwide.

pages.title: Poch Characteristics
facts: There are several characteristics which can be seen on most of the Poch figures.
These characteristics can of course also appear on other figures which are not produced in Spain.
It's important for me to stress that not every figure with dents, melt-marks, “dripped” paint or faded/discolored hands is assumed to be a POCH variant.
As you can see in the pictures above all “Poch” produced pale hands are noticeably similar in appearance.
A. It only appears on the limbs (“soft” plastic), never on a torso (“hard” plastic).
B. It was only found in black or white/pale sprayed areas.
C. The thickness of the paint seems to affect this phenomenon. It never occurs in thinly sprayed areas.
After studying these marks for a while I have found out that you can find mainly three different types of melt marks

facts: This guide is dedicated to the mould-colour variants produced by Kenner in the Asian factories (Taiwan, Macau, Smile, Unitoy and Kader).
Changes to mould-colour could occur during production or simply because different factories were involved.
It is worth noting that most vintage Star Wars figures have limbs made from two different colours (one painted, one moulded).
The factory then had to choose: Do I mould the arms in “colour A” and paint it with “colour B” or the other way around?
This is the 2021 reworked edition of this guide. I hope you enjoy it.
If you want to spot a “white moulded legs” Han Solo take a look at the peg holes and look for tiny rubs to the feet or to the hip.

facts: So what is a baggie? Why & where were they available, and why would one want to collect them rather than loose figures or carded ones?
So baggie is the term used for figures that were issued either directly or indirectly to the public in little plastic bags rather than the traditional carded figures
They were available in various ways, usually in the form of card back promotions like the single figure mail-aways (Dengar/Survival kit/Boba Fett etc.) where you would save up
They were a way to buy several figures in a cheaper format than you would buying regular carded figures on hangers in store.
Heat sealed Either sealed one end or both ends on a heat sealing machine
Tape sealed Taped closed at one end usually with a heat seal at the other

Does the heat seal look right?
Is the heat seal messy & disjointed.

Is the font the correct size/colour & print style as a know legit example?

Is the tape clean clear? Obviously some yellow, but it is too clear if there is such a thing?

pages.title: Palitoy Cardbacks
facts: This guide intends to categorise all of the different packaging types used by the Palitoy company in the UK for Star Wars action figures from the original set
The early cards were manufactured in Asia by the Palitoy (Far East) Ltd company in Hong Kong at the Kader Industries factory and shipped back assembled to the
The Kader Industries factory also produced Kenner cards and the same bubbles and figures can be seen on both Palitoy and Kenner cards for the earlier cards.
N = No factory code on 41A and 41B which is used to identify cards with no factory code on the back of the card
B = black background which is used to distinguish between the two ESB 45-back Bounty Hunter Offer variations
G = HG, N = HN, T = HT which are letters that follow (ROTJ/1) and (ROTJ/2) on the bottom right hand corner of the back of ROTJ cards
K = PBP Tri -Logo card with a Tri-Logo back with updated addresses
Each entry on the matrix can be 1 of 4 possible values
” ” - an empty space denotes a cardback/figure variation which is known to have never existed
“-” - a dash indicates a cardback/figure variation which may or may not exist, there is no known example
“?” - indicates a cardback/figure variation which has been reported as existing but not verified
“X” - indicates a cardback/figure variation which has a known example
